name: Color
description: Color system for application surfaces, text, borders, interactions, status, feedback, and expressive accents.
rationale: Use a restrained neutral foundation with amethyst as the primary identity and interaction color. Supporting teal, blue, raspberry, and purple colors provide secondary and expressive options without competing with semantic meaning. Semantic roles reference a small primitive palette so product code expresses intent rather than raw hues. Every interactive role carries its own hover, pressed, selected, and disabled values, and every fill role has a verified foreground, so agents never have to invent a state color or guess whether white text is legible on a given surface. Identity fills sit close to the 4.5:1 floor because their hues are fixed; every role Monet derived rather than inherited is pushed clear of the floor so a state change or a tinted surface cannot drop a legible pairing below it. Dark mode is the same system resolved on dark surfaces rather than a second palette: every semantic role keeps its meaning, fills and their verified foregrounds keep their exact values, and only the surfaces, text, borders, tints, and focus color move, each to a primitive chosen to clear the same contrast margins on the dark surfaces it is documented against.
guidance:
Use semantic color roles in product code rather than raw palette values. Use amethyst for primary interactive emphasis. Reserve red for destructive actions and errors, blue for informational meaning, teal for success, and amber for warnings. Use bright purple, soft teal, and raspberry primarily as expressive accents, highlights, visualization colors, or subtle selected states.

Filled surfaces: pair every fill with its verified foreground — color.on.primary, color.on.secondary, color.on.accent, color.on.highlight, color.on.info, color.on.success, color.on.warning, and color.on.danger. Do not assume white is legible; teal, the expressive purple, and other light fills take a dark foreground.

Tinted surfaces: use the .surface variants of info, success, warning, and danger for alerts, banners, and quiet status regions. These are light enough to carry ordinary color.foreground text, so do not also switch the text to a status color.

Status text: every status has a fill and a text role. color.info, color.success, color.warning, and color.danger are fills that carry their color.on.* foreground; color.info.foreground, color.success.foreground, color.warning.foreground, and color.danger.foreground are the text and icon colors, verified on color.surface in both modes. On a tinted status surface keep the text color.foreground and let the icon or indicator carry the status color, as the Badge and Alert decisions say. In light mode the info, warning, and danger pairs share a value, so nothing changes visually; in dark mode the fills stay put and the text roles lighten. color.primary is an interaction and fill color rather than a text color on tinted surfaces; use color.primary.foreground for amethyst text, icons, and selection indicators.

Interaction: quiet surfaces move color.surface to color.surface.hover and color.surface.pressed; filled primary and destructive controls move to their .hover and .pressed values. Selection uses color.surface.selected with color.primary.foreground for its text, icon, or indicator, and color.primary for a solid selected fill or rail. Disabled controls use color.surface.disabled and color.foreground.disabled.

Text placement: body and status text belongs on color.surface, where every semantic text role is verified in both modes. Against color.background, only color.foreground and color.foreground.muted are guaranteed, so keep status, link, and accent text on a surface rather than directly on the page background. color.foreground.muted is verified against color.surface and every state surface, including color.surface.pressed, in light and dark.

Boundaries: Monet has one border decision and three border colors. color.border.subtle is a quiet separator inside a surface. color.border is the boundary of non-interactive structure — panels, cards, table rules, and section edges — and does not on its own meet the 3:1 non-text minimum. color.border.strong is the resting boundary of an unfilled control: a text input, textarea, select trigger, search field, password field, combobox, checkbox box, or radio circle, whose boundary is the only thing identifying it as interactive. A control that carries its own fill — a filled button, a checked checkbox, a selected segmented item — is identified by the fill and keeps the structural border or no border at all. The Borders foundation owns the matching stroke widths and references these same colors.

Verify normal text at a minimum 4.5:1 contrast ratio and meaningful non-text boundaries at 3:1. Roles Monet derived rather than inherited from the identity palette are held to a 4.75:1 safety margin against the surfaces they are documented on, so a later tint or state change cannot quietly cross the floor. Never rely on color alone to communicate meaning.

Modes: the same semantic roles resolve in light and dark; product code never branches on mode, it uses the role and lets resolution pick the value. Fills — color.primary and its states, color.danger and its states, color.info, color.success, color.warning, color.secondary, color.accent, color.highlight — and every color.on.* foreground are identical in both modes, so a filled button or badge is the same object on a dark screen. What changes in dark mode: surfaces and their hover, pressed, selected, and disabled states move to the dark neutrals and a deep amethyst tint; color.foreground, color.foreground.muted, and color.foreground.disabled lighten; borders move to the dark neutrals while color.border.strong keeps its 3:1 boundary contrast; the tinted status surfaces become deep tints that still carry color.foreground; the status text roles, color.link, color.primary.foreground, and color.focus lighten to keep 4.75:1 on the dark surfaces. Hover and pressed on fills still darken in both modes, because a fill's contrast is measured against its own foreground, not the surface. Shadows and the modal scrim strengthen in dark mode; see Elevation and Opacity.
notes:
Preferred palette: amethyst #9B59B6, bright purple #DC95FF, turquoise #1ABC9C, soft teal #7AE2CF, blue #3498DB, raspberry #CF4173, danger red #D0311E, dark blue-gray #2C3E50, light neutral #ECF0F1, and white #FFFFFF. Amber is included specifically to provide a distinct warning state.

Identity hues are fixed, so color.on.primary, color.on.secondary, color.on.accent, and color.on.success land just above the 4.5:1 floor by design. Every role Monet derived was moved clear of it instead: color.link and color.info left blue.500 (3.15:1 on white) for blue.600, color.warning left amber.600 (3.64:1 on white) for amber.700, and those two derived steps plus teal.700 were then darkened again so status text, the white-on-warning fill, and success text all clear 5:1 rather than sitting a rounding error above the minimum. neutral.600 was darkened for the same reason: as color.foreground.muted it fell to 4.43:1 on color.surface.pressed, and as color.border.strong it is the boundary an unfilled control depends on. The identity values remain available as primitives for expressive and visualization use. color.success intentionally keeps turquoise because it is an identity color; its dark foreground pairing and a separate color.success.foreground cover the contrast requirement instead.

color.primary.foreground exists because color.primary reaches only 4.01:1 on color.surface.selected, and selection guidance depends on amethyst text and indicators being readable there. It parallels color.success.foreground: the same identity hue, one step darker, for text rather than fill.

color.border.subtle completes the border family so the Borders foundation can reference a Color role for every stroke instead of carrying its own hexes.

Hover and pressed steps are derived by darkening the base role rather than by overlaying opacity, so the resulting color stays predictable on any surface. Add another interaction step only when a recurring component need cannot be met by hover, pressed, selected, and disabled.

Dark mode adds a cool blue-gray ramp below neutral.900 — neutral.925, .950, and .975 — plus neutral.350, .500, and .800, because the light ramp's warm grays sit at the wrong luminances for dark surfaces: neutral.400 falls to 4.1:1 as muted text on the dark pressed surface, so muted text and the control boundary use neutral.350, which clears 5.3:1 there and 7.5:1 on color.surface. The status text roles use a 400 step of each hue: blue.400, amber.400, and red.400 each clear 6:1 on the dark surface and on their deep 900 tint, and teal.300 already does. Identity fills keep their light values in dark mode because their verified pairings are with their own foregrounds: amethyst on the dark surface is 3.3:1, which also satisfies the non-text minimum for a selection rail. Deep tints (purple.900, blue.900, teal.900, amber.900, red.900) are chosen so color.foreground stays above 12:1 and each status text role above 5.9:1 on them.

tokens.name: color.danger

tokens.name: color.focus
tokens.description: Visible keyboard-focus indicator, held to the 3:1 non-text minimum against color.surface in both modes.
